text: A trained model is a black box by default. Two people can hand you the same file and neither can tell you what it was trained on or where it falls apart, without digging through notebooks and Slack history. Model documentation closes that gap.

A model card is a short, structured document that ships alongside a model, popularized by a 2019 Google paper and now the default shape across the industry. A card like this one names the model, its intended use, what it's explicitly not validated for, a summary of its training data, its evaluation metrics, known limitations, and who owns it.

Six sections matter. Intended use, what task and who the users are. Out-of-scope use, uses it was explicitly not validated for, the line that stops a marketing segmentation model from quietly getting reused for credit decisions. Training data and evaluation, sources and metrics, often broken out by subgroup. Known limitations and an owner, where it underperforms, and who's accountable for keeping the card current.

A model card serves two audiences at once. Builders and reviewers need the technical detail, data sources, metrics, limitations, to debug an issue or reconstruct what happened months ago. Affected stakeholders, a compliance officer, a regulator, sometimes the person the model decided about, need the plain-language version, what this model is allowed to decide and what it was never supposed to be used for.

The out-of-scope-use section is usually the one that prevents the worst incidents, because it's the line that stops a model from drifting into a use case nobody validated. Next up: model inventory and registry, keeping track of every model an organization has.
